chunk_findings.detail: `_non_negative_float` accepts any value `>= 0`, including non-finite and absurdly large finite floats. A `[suites]` config with `load_poll_s = 1e308` (or `inf` if the TOML parser admits it) passes validation because `1e308 >= 0` is true and the function returns `""`. Since this knob is documented as the number of seconds between host-load readings while a suite is waiting for admission, a waiting suite can then sleep effectively forever before the next admission check, so the suite-lock wait is not bounded. The validation should require a finite number and/or impose a sane upper bound on the polling interval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/suites.py:`_non_negative_float` / `load_poll_s`

chunk_findings.detail: `running` now scans only `range(limit(cfg))`, so a process whose current limit is smaller than the limit under which other live suites acquired slots will not see those holders. The lock state is shared across projects/agents, so if project A has `[suites].max_concurrent = 20` and holds slot 10, while project B has the default limit 1, project B's `running(cfg)` checks only slot 0, reports no running suites, and `load_block(..., running=0)` returns `""` because of the “lone suite” exception. Project B can then admit into slot 0, creating two concurrent suites and bypassing the load budget. The scan needs to cover all live slots (or a stable maximum), not just slots below the caller’s current cap.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:149 (`running`)

chunk_findings.detail: The loop caches the result of `load_block` for up to `cfg.suites.load_poll_s` seconds and then uses that cached `reason` to decide whether to attempt `slots.hold`. If the first head-of-queue check finds load below the ceiling but all slots are held, `reason` is set to `""` and `reason_at` is updated. If host load then rises above the ceiling and a slot is released before `load_poll_s` elapses, the next iteration still sees `reason == ""`, skips the load re-read because `CLOCK.monotonic() - reason_at < poll_s`, and calls `slots.hold(slots_n, 0)`, admitting the suite even though the current load is over the budget. The same stale cache can also keep a suite blocked after load clears. A load-budget admission check should be performed immediately before an acquisition attempt (or at least whenever a slot becomes free); `load_poll_s` should rate-limit repeated checks while blocked, not allow admission on a stale “not blocked” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py: `suite_lock` load-reason cache

chunk_findings.detail: The help says the concurrency cap is derived from cores but is “never under `[ci].max_concurrent_suites`”. If `max_concurrent_suites` has its natural meaning as an upper bound, using it as a lower bound makes the lock admit more suites than the core budget. On a 4-core host with the new default `[suites].cores_per_suite = 96` (so the core-derived count is 0/1) and `[ci].max_concurrent_suites = 8`, the documented behavior admits 8 suites at once when load is initially low, despite the same config saying each suite should have 96 cores. That is a wrong admission/overload path; the CI maximum should cap the derived value, not floor it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/parallel.md:90

chunk_findings.detail: The added `cfg.suites.max_concurrent = 1` makes these tests deterministic only for the core-derived cap; it does not isolate the new host-load budget. The tests still create `Config()` with only `XDG_STATE_HOME` overridden, so `suites.load_ceiling_per_core` remains whatever default or user config supplies. Given a host whose load average exceeds the load ceiling (or a user config such as `[suites] load_ceiling_per_core = 0.1`), `SL.hold(...)` or the subsequent acquisition can be blocked by load even though `max_concurrent` is forced to one slot, causing tests such as `test_a_wait_override_extends_the_suite_wait_knob` and the tests in `test_gate_run_timeout_suite_lock_wait.py` to fail or time out for the wrong reason. To model “one slot” hermetically, the tests should also disable/neutralize the load budget (e.g. set the documented disabled value for `load_ceiling_per_core`, or monkeypatch `os.getloadavg`/`load_block`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_suite_lock.py:_cfg

chunk_findings.detail: The test creates the second suite with `cfg()`, whose `suites.load_poll_s` is `0.0`, but then asserts that after `time.sleep(0.3)` the thread has not been admitted. If `load_poll_s=0` is honored as “poll without sleeping” (which the non-negative knob allows and the helper explicitly sets), the thread can read the three fake load samples `0.9, 0.9, 0.2` and enter the context in far less than `0.3` s, so `assert order == []` fails nondeterministically. The test needs a positive poll interval or explicit synchronization instead of relying on thread scheduling.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_suite_load_budget.py:test_the_second_suite_starts_once_the_load_falls

chunk_findings.detail: This test also uses `cfg()` with `load_poll_s=0.0`, while its comment and `>=0.2` assertion assume a `0.25` s poll; with immediate polling the four fake load samples can be consumed before `0.2` s and the assertion can fail. Separately, the final assertion `time.monotonic() - marks["admitted"] < time.monotonic() - marks["queued"]` is always true whenever `marks["admitted"]` is set after `marks["queued"]`, so it cannot detect a per-test clock that incorrectly includes queue time; it is vacuous.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_suite_load_budget.py:test_waiting_for_load_is_queue_time_not_run_time

chunk_findings.detail: `test_waiting_for_load_is_queue_time_not_run_time` builds `cfg()` with `load_poll_s=0` and a source of three over-ceiling samples then `0.1`, then requires `marks["admitted"] - marks["queued"] >= 0.2` because “poll is 0.25 s”. The fixture never sets 0.25. If `hold` honors `load_poll_s=0`, those samples are consumed with no quarter-second sleeps, admission is well under 0.2 s, and the assertion fails even though the waiter behaved as configured. The bound does not match the input the test passes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_suite_load_budget.py:131

chunk_findings.detail: The follow-up `time.monotonic() - marks["admitted"] < time.monotonic() - marks["queued"]` does not start a per-test run clock and does not show that queue time was excluded from one (DX-ci-timeout-excludes-queue). With a single `now`, it is exactly `admitted > queued`. Two `monotonic()` reads only make it flaky when the wait is shorter than the gap between the calls. A run clock that still includes the load wait still passes.

chunk_findings.detail: `load_block` only treats `None` as an unreadable load, but other common missing/invalid load values still cause a wrong hold. Given `running=1`, `cfg.suites.load_ceiling_per_core=1.0`, and a `SignalSource` whose `sample()` returns `{"load": float("nan")}` (a usual representation of an unreadable metric), the check `value is None or value <= ceiling` evaluates to `False` because `nan <= 1.0` is false. The function then returns a block reason and holds the suite, even though the docstring says an unreadable load never blocks.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:load_block

chunk_findings.detail: While a reason is cached, `check` returns `self.reason` without re-reading `_held` or calling `load_block`. Since the class docstring says the running-slot count is one of the things that keeps the head out, and `self.running` is passed into `load_block`, a slot that frees during the cached interval is invisible. For example, with `[suites].load_poll_s = 10`, one suite holding the only slot, and `load_block` blocking because `running=1`, the head waiter caches the block. If the holder exits after 1 second, `_held(slot)` is now false and the budget would admit, but for the remaining 9 seconds `check` still returns the cached reason, so `hold` continues to wait; with `wait_s=5` it raises `SuiteBusy` even though the lock is free.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:_Admission.check

chunk_findings.detail: The initial timestamp sentinel is the finite value `-1e9`. `check` performs a load read only when `CLOCK.monotonic() - self._at >= self.poll_s`. On a freshly booted host where `CLOCK.monotonic()` starts near 0, a configured positive `load_poll_s` larger than about 1e9 seconds (or a non-finite value such as `inf`/`NaN` if the seconds validator lets it through) makes this condition false on the first call. `check` then returns the initial empty reason and never calls `load_block`, admitting a suite even when the host load is over the ceiling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:_Admission.__init__

chunk_findings.detail: The helper defaults `poll=0.0`, and `test_the_poll_knob_is_bounded` asserts `_poll_seconds(0) == ""` (so zero is an accepted poll value), yet timing tests call `cfg()` and assume a 0.25-second poll. If `load_poll_s=0` is honored as zero, `test_the_second_suite_starts_once_the_load_falls` fails because the second thread consumes `0.9, 0.9, 0.2` immediately and is admitted before the main thread’s `time.sleep(0.3)`, so `assert order == []` is false. The same misconfiguration makes `test_waiting_for_load_is_queue_time_not_run_time` assert a wait of at least 0.2 seconds while explicitly configuring no polling delay.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_suite_load_budget.py:cfg

chunk_findings.detail: The test uses `time.sleep(0.5)` to assume the waiter thread has already consumed the first `FakeSource` value while both slots are held, but there is no synchronization guaranteeing that interleaving. On a loaded CI, the thread may not run until after `b` exits; it then sees a free slot, reads the first source value `0.1` (under the 0.35 ceiling), and is admitted. `outcome[0]` becomes `"admitted"`, and the assertion `"load" in outcome[0]` fails.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_suite_load_budget.py:test_a_slot_freed_while_the_load_is_over_the_ceiling_is_not_taken

chunk_findings.detail: `hold(cfg(), ...)` sets `load_poll_s=0` (the helper default), but the assertion requires `marks["admitted"] - marks["queued"] >= 0.2` and the comment claims a 0.25 s poll. With source `load(0.9, 0.9, 0.9, 0.1)`, a zero poll drains those samples in one tight loop, so the measured wait is far under 0.2 s and the test fails even though admission is correct. The follow-up `time.monotonic() - marks["admitted"] < wait` is also not a per-test clock started at admission: if join/scheduling after the `with` exceeds that short wait, it fails the other way. Neither check shows that queue time is excluded from run time.
